On startup, Paws runs `recoverOnStartup` (`src/db/recovery.ts`), which inspects every work item in the startup states `awaiting_input`, `running`, `verifying`, `recovering`, and `merge_queue` and decides, per item, what to do with the work the shutdown interrupted (`src/db/recovery.ts:51-57`) (`src/db/recovery.ts:31-37`). Before deciding anything, it first calls `shiftRunnerLeasesForDowntime`, because the doc comment says Paws downtime up to an `offlineBudgetMs` does not count against an open runner lease (`src/db/recovery.ts:44-52`). Each in-flight item then goes through `decideStartup`, and a restart is safe mid-work: the README says runners keep working while Paws is down and Paws reattaches to the same commands after startup, including in-flight Closeout reviews and answer tasks (`README.md:54`) (`src/core/recovery.ts:75-83`).

Per-item outcome, as computed by `decideStartup` in `src/core/recovery.ts` and applied via `applyDecision` in `src/db/decisions.ts`:

1. **Merge queue items keep their place** (`keep_place`): a queued item whose run is not still active stays in `merge_queue` (`src/core/recovery.ts:95-96`). Its merge job is re-armed in `applyKeepPlace`: an open merge job gets its `run_at` pulled to now (and flagged `mergeCallInFlight` if a merge call was in flight — `mergeCallInFlight` checks the `merge_call` table (`src/db/remote-merges.ts:78-80`)); otherwise the last merge job's payload is re-queued (`src/db/decisions.ts:143-177`). A merge call that may have been in flight makes the job run now and, per the code comment, "ask GitHub first: merged records the merge, anything else re-verifies" (`src/db/decisions.ts:138-141`). This matches the recovery doc comment: "An item in the merge queue keeps its place; one whose merge call may have been in flight asks GitHub before it moves" (`src/db/recovery.ts:42-44`). If the run was still active in the lane when the process died, the item re-verifies instead of keeping its place (`src/core/recovery.ts:94-97`) (`src/core/recovery.test.ts:122-142`).

2. **Running/verifying items are resumed once** — per the doc comment, from their checkpoint or, without one, from their branch, in a fresh session; if a runner still holds the item's work, the resume reattaches to that work (`reattach: true`) (`src/core/recovery.ts:76-100`) (`src/db/recovery.ts:75-78`). Resumes are staggered 5 seconds apart (`STARTUP_RESUME_SPACING_MS`) via `nextResumeAt` so a batch of restarts doesn't start all at once [E1:56,85] (`src/db/recovery.ts:39`). A verifying item whose runner still holds its Closeout review or check run, or whose merge was in progress, re-verifies instead [E4:97-98,103-104]; `applyReverify` cancels open jobs, rewinds a `merge_queue` checkpoint to `verifying`, and enqueues a `reverify` job with `recheckHead: true, failClosed: true` (`src/db/decisions.ts:113-136`). A re-verify the shutdown cut short attaches to the runner's Closeout work itself rather than double-scheduling (`src/db/recovery.ts:75-82`).

3. **Crash-loop guard**: an item that was already resumed once (recoveryAttempts ≥ 1) and it hasn't yet been long enough since that resume (`sinceResumeMs < RESUME_AGAIN_AFTER_MS`, value not in the evidence) gets `ask_restart` — the docs say the next start still unfinished asks in Linear whether to start it again [E4:77-78,101-102] (`src/core/recovery.test.ts:82-109`),(`src/core/recovery.test.ts:92-108`). No checkpoint but a first attempt still resumes; a second attempt without a checkpoint also asks (`src/core/recovery.test.ts:111-120`).

4. **Skipped items**: an item with a parked capacity wait (a pending start/resume/reverify job carrying a `capacityWait` payload) is left alone — the comment says restarting "neither spends recovery nor adds a job" since its next attempt already exists [E1:62,103-114]. Same for items with a pending answer resume or pending transient retry (`src/db/recovery.ts:63-64`).

5. **Open questions**: `awaiting_input` items have their run capacity released, and if any are awaiting input a `catchup` job (`startup-questions:<now>`) is enqueued once so questions are re-surfaced (`src/db/recovery.ts:89-98`).

Top-level flow: `src/index.ts` imports `recoverOnStartup` (and `markPawsAlive`/`prepareShutdown`) (`src/index.ts:104-107`); the evidence shows the export from `src/db` but not the exact call site in `src/index.ts`, so the call timing at boot is an inference. The job and outbox loops run via `startLoops` with 64 workers (`src/db/loops.ts:12-33`), so the resume/reverify/merge jobs created by `applyDecision` execute after the startup decisions commit. Separately, `restart` in `src/db/restart.ts` refuses while a merge call is still in flight — per its doc comment, the merge lane owns the item until GitHub confirms the outcome (`src/db/restart.ts:20-31`); who invokes `restart` on the recovery path was not shown in the evidence.

On a second restart, a still-unfinished item that was already resumed once is not silently resumed again — Paws asks in Linear whether to start it again (`ask_restart`). (`src/core/recovery.ts:77-79`, `src/core/recovery.ts:99-100`)

Concretely, `decideStartup` checks the item's `recoveryAttempts` count: if it is at least 1 and the time since the item was last resumed (`sinceResumeMs`, derived from `item.resumedAt` in `recoverOnStartup`) is still within `RESUME_AGAIN_AFTER_MS`, the decision is `ask_restart`. (`src/core/recovery.ts:99-100`) In `recoverOnStartup`, that decision is applied normally via `applyDecision`, unless a runner still holds the item's work (which takes the reattach path first) or the item already has a pending answer/retry/capacity-wait parked. (`src/db/recovery.ts:58-87`)

There are some shortcuts where the "ask again" is skipped on the second restart: a runner still holding the work yields a `resume` with `reattach: true` (no recovery attempt spent, attaching to the existing work). [E1:97-100, E4:22-26 test] A `verifying` item whose runner still holds its Closeout review or check run re-verifies and attaches to that work, regardless of `recoveryAttempts`. (`src/core/recovery.ts:81-82`, `src/core/recovery.ts:96`) An `ensureRestartQuestion` call at the start of the per-item loop also short-circuits into an `ask_restart` decision if a restart question was already created for the item. (`src/db/recovery.ts:55-58`)

So the general case the question asks about is: the item was already resumed once after the previous restart, the runner no longer holds it, and it is still unfinished — then the second startup produces an `ask_restart` decision, meaning Paws asks in Linear whether to start it again rather than resuming a second time. (`src/core/recovery.ts:77-79`, `src/core/recovery.ts:99-100`)

answer.text:
Short answer: Paws does not silently resume the task a second time. On the next start, `decideStartup` sees `recoveryAttempts >= 1` and, when little time has passed since the first resume (or no `resumedAt` was recorded, so `sinceResumeMs` defaults to 0), returns an `ask_restart`: Paws asks in the item's Linear session whether to start the task again from its branch, and only a person's answer restarts it.

The flow at startup: `recoverOnStartup` in `src/db/recovery.ts` lists items in the startup states (`awaiting_input`, `running`, `verifying`, `recovering`, `merge_queue`) (`src/db/recovery.ts:31-37`), shifts runner leases by the downtime, and skips items that already have a restart question standing (via `ensureRestartQuestion`), a parked capacity wait, a pending answer resume, or a pending transient-failure retry (`src/db/recovery.ts:57-64`). For the rest it calls `decideStartup`, passing `item.recoveryAttempts` and, if the item has a `resumedAt`, `sinceResumeMs = now - item.resumedAt` (`src/db/recovery.ts:66-74`).

Inside `decideStartup` (`src/core/recovery.ts`) the doc comment states the policy: "A running or verifying item is resumed once in a fresh session... The next start, still unfinished, asks in Linear whether to start it again" (`src/core/recovery.ts:76-78`). The code implements this at (`src/core/recovery.ts:101-102`): when `recoveryAttempts >= 1` and `(sinceResumeMs?? 0) < RESUME_AGAIN_AFTER_MS`, it returns `{ type: "ask_restart" }`. So the once-resumed item is routed to the question only while it is still inside that window; the value of `RESUME_AGAIN_AFTER_MS` is not in the inspected evidence. Below that check, a verifying item with a verification candidate would get a `reverify` and otherwise a plain `resume` (`src/core/recovery.ts:103-105`), but a once-resumed item inside the window never reaches those lines.

Applying the decision: `applyAskRestart` in `src/db/decisions.ts` handles it. If the item has no `sessionKey`, it fails the item outright with reason `resume_already_attempted` and message "Stopped after a restart because this run was already resumed once." (`src/db/decisions.ts:92-102`). Otherwise it expires the lease, records a restart hold via `holdRestart`, and — unless the question already stands or is queued — cancels open jobs for the item, releases run capacity, and posts the restart question (`src/db/decisions.ts:103-111`), reusing the existing question where one stands (`src/db/decisions.ts:107`, `src/db/restart-hold.ts:32-42`). The question text lives in `src/db/restart-hold.ts`: "Paws restarted twice while this task was running. Start it again from its branch in a fresh session? Stop the session to leave it." with a single "Start again" option (`src/db/restart-hold.ts:5-8`, `src/db/restart-hold.ts:55-71`). If Paws restarts yet again while the hold stands, `ensureRestartQuestion` matches the hold and returns true, so `recoverOnStartup` records another `ask_restart` without duplicating the question (`src/db/recovery.ts:58-61`, `src/db/restart-hold.ts:55-58`) — though `restartHold` only returns a hold for items in `recovering` or `awaiting_input` (`src/db/restart-hold.ts:10-21`), so this depends on the item having moved into one of those states after the lease expired, which the evidence shows only as inference. The item stays suspended until a person answers; there is no automatic second resume.

Exceptions and edge cases worth noting:
1. If the runner still holds the item's work, that check comes earlier in `decideStartup`'s if-chain than the `recoveryAttempts >= 1` branch [E1:98-100 vs E1:101], so a runner-held item re-attaches to the running work (or, in `verifying`, re-verifies and attaches to its Closeout work) rather than being asked (`src/core/recovery.ts:98-100`). The `recoveryAttempts` check sits after the runner-held and merge-queue branches but before the plain resume/reverify fallback.
2. Merge-queue items: if the run was not active, the item keeps its queue place and the merge job first asks GitHub whether an in-flight merge went through (`src/core/recovery.ts:94-96`); if a merge was in progress per the checkpoint, it re-verifies (`src/core/recovery.ts:97`, `src/core/recovery.ts:71-73`). These take precedence over the ask-restart path for merge-queue items.
3. Skipped items: capacity waits, pending answer resumes, and pending transient-failure retries are left untouched — a capacity wait "already has its next attempt; restarting neither spends recovery nor adds a job" (`src/db/recovery.ts:62-64`, `src/db/recovery.ts:103-114`).
4. When the person answers, the answer path goes through `restart` in `src/db/restart.ts`, which halts the item, ends the run, resets counters (and clears the cancellation fence for a failed item), requeues a resume job carrying the handoff text and, for fix reasons, tracks fix rounds against `latestHumanTurn` (`src/db/restart.ts:25-84`, `src/db/restart.ts:97-109`); `pendingRestartHandoff` recovers the latest unfinished agent input so a later resume job carries the prior handoff (`src/db/restart.ts:128-145`). That handoff/limit plumbing in `pendingRestartHandoff` reaches `applyResume`'s resume-job payload (`src/db/decisions.ts:84`), which applies to the plain-resume (outside-window or first-time) case.

answer.text:
On SIGTERM, Paws runs a single-shot shutdown handler and reaps in-flight work rather than abandoning it: WIP is committed on each in-flight item branch, running/verifying items are moved to a recovering state without consuming a resume attempt, and merge-queue items with an active run are marked lost. The signal doesn't panic; it deliberately preserves what a runner still holds.

Concretely, in `src/index.ts` the SIGTERM handler (and SIGINT) calls `shutdown()`, which guards against double-fire via an `exiting` flag and then invokes `shutdownPaws(paws, exitCode)` (`src/index.ts:2055-2061`). The recovery path, `prepareShutdown` in `src/db/recovery.ts`, documents and implements the work-item behavior: "SIGINT / SIGTERM. Commit WIP on each in-flight item branch, then move running work to recovering without using the one resume attempt. Work a runner still holds keeps its state: an agent turn, or a verifying item's Closeout review or check run" (`src/db/recovery.ts:165-172`).

The steps in `prepareShutdown` are:
1. If a `commitWip` callback is provided, it is called for each item from `listInFlightItems(db)`; a failure there is journaled and skipped, because "a missing worktree is not a reason to skip shutdown" — the lease move still happens (`src/db/recovery.ts:178-187`).
2. Inside an immediate transaction it marks Paws alive, then lists work items in `running` and `verifying` states (`src/db/recovery.ts:188-190`).
3. For each such item, if it's in a parked capacity wait or `runnerHoldsWork` (a run whose work a runner actively holds), it is skipped and keeps its state (`src/db/recovery.ts:192`, `src/db/recovery.ts:208-214`). Otherwise the current run (if any) is marked `lost`, and unless the item keeps verification, a `lease_expired` work-item event is applied (`src/db/recovery.ts:193-194`).
4. For items in `merge_queue`, only those whose current run is still `active` get the run marked `lost` and a `lease_expired` event; per the doc comment, a merge-queue item "keeps its state and its place for the next start to pick up; one whose run is still active is left for a re-verify" [E1:196-200, 170-171].

A test under `test/shutdown-wip.test.ts` confirms the end-to-end effect: a queued item with an implement run, when the process is killed with SIGTERM, exits with code 0, its worktree's last commit subject becomes "wip: shutdown", and the item's state after restart is `recovering` (`test/shutdown-wip.test.ts:249-262`).

What we don't see: the body of `shutdownPaws` (which presumably wires `prepareShutdown` into the shutdown path), how the signal handler passes the `commitWip` callback, and the semantics of `runnerHoldsRunWork` beyond that it consults `cancelRequested` and a grace window (`ORPHAN_GRACE_MS`, 5 minutes) — so the exact path from the SIGTERM handler to `prepareShutdown` is inferred, not shown.

answer.text:
Paws answers SIGTERM by stopping all component groups, committing each in-flight item's worktree as a 'wip: shutdown' checkpoint, and then in one SQLite transaction marking its run lost and moving running/verifying items a runner no longer holds into 'recovering' via the lease_expired event — without consuming their one resume attempt — while items the runner still holds and items waiting on parked capacity keep their state, and merge-queue items keep their state and place unless their run is still active, in which case the run is marked lost and they move to recovering too. It then closes the database and exits, with exit code 1 if the durable state flush failed. See inside for the full trace.

The wiring: src/index.ts installs process.on("SIGTERM") handlers that callShutdown, which invokes `shutdownPaws(paws, 0)` exactly once (`src/index.ts:2054-2061`). That calls `paws.stop()`, which in src/index.ts's startPaws return object runs `stopPawsComponents` (`src/index.ts:1544-1584`). Stages run in groups — abort the runner abort signal and stop the host; then Linear, server, reconciler, orchestrator; then job/outbox loops; then workspace; then runner — each stage raced against a 5-second per-stage timeout (STOP_WAIT_MS, chosen to stay under systemd's stop deadline) [E7:4,30-43]. After all groups, the flush step calls `prepareShutdown(db, Date.now(), commitWip)` (`src/index.ts:1567-1577`), and finally the close step clears the alive timer and closes SQLite (`src/index.ts:1578-1581`). Even after a stage failure, flush and close still run; failures are collected into a `PawsStopError` (`src/shutdown.ts:19-57`).

What happens to the work items (`src/db/recovery.ts:165-202`), inside `prepareShutdown`:
1. If a WIP-commit hook is supplied, it is applied to each in-flight item. A failure is journaled and skipped — the comment says a missing worktree is not a reason to skip shutdown, and the lease move still happens (`src/db/recovery.ts:178-187`). The hook installed in src/index.ts commits "wip: shutdown" to the item's worktree using the run's stored commit policy, if it has one (`src/index.ts:1568-1576`).
2. In a single `immediate` transaction, with a final `markPawsAlive`, it lists "running" and "verifying" items. Items that have parked capacity-wait or whose runner still holds the work (an agent turn, or a verifying item's Closeout review or check run, kept via `keepsVerification`) are skipped entirely. Otherwise the run is marked "lost" and, unless the item keeps verification, the "lease_expired" event moves it to recovering (`src/db/recovery.ts:188-195`). The recovery docs say recovering work does not use the one resume attempt (`src/db/recovery.ts:166-168`).
3. Merge-queue items are handled separately: only those whose run is still active are marked lost and moved via "lease_expired"; a queued item whose run is finished keeps its state and its place for the next start [E1:196-200,204-206].

The exit path: `shutdownPaws` journals each failed stage and downgrades the exit code to 1 unless the error is a PawsStopError whose state was still flushed successfully; otherwise it exits with the requested code (0 for SIGTERM) (`src/shutdown.ts:61-77`). A SIGTERM during startup stops what `paws.ready` waits on and the process parks until that shutdown chooses the exit code (`src/index.ts:2074-2083`). The shutdown-wip test confirms the observable behavior: killing with SIGTERM exits 0, leaves a "wip: shutdown" commit on the item branch, and the item ends in state "recovering" (`test/shutdown-wip.test.ts:249-262`).

answer.text:
A Linear webhook delivery arrives at `handleLinearWebhook` (src/linear/webhook.ts) and becomes orchestrator work only after passing verification, dedupe, and persistence, after which it is dispatched either to an intake queue or fired as a fire-and-forget `onEvent` callback. The flow is:

1. **Verify**: The delivery's `linear-signature` header must be a 64-hex HMAC; the secret must be configured, the HMAC must match the raw body, and the timestamp (`webhookTimestamp` from the body, falling back to the `linear-timestamp` header) must be within `TIMESTAMP_WINDOW_MS` of 60 seconds (`src/linear/webhook.ts:17`, `src/linear/webhook.ts:64-72`, `src/linear/webhook.ts:112-138`). Verification failures are counted per inbox via `noteFailure` and answered with a 401 (400 for bad payloads) (`src/linear/webhook.ts:139`, `src/linear/webhook.ts:173-180`).
2. **Parse**: `parseAgentEvent` extracts the session/issue/activity IDs, body, and derives an `action` (`created`, `prompted`, etc.), a `signal` (a `stop` signal comes from an archived/dismissed/stopping session or a Paws stop body), and a `dedupeKey` built from action, session, activity, and delivery ID (`src/linear/webhook.ts:198-255`).
3. **Persist and ack**: If a store is present, the handler sets the `linear:webhook` cursor (used by the silent-webhook watchdog in src/db/linear-webhook.ts (`src/db/linear-webhook.ts:15-29`)) and commits the event, which returns whether it was newly inserted and previously handled. The HTTP 200 is returned without awaiting any follow-up, to stay within Linear's 5-second ack budget (`src/linear/webhook.ts:102-106`, `src/linear/webhook.ts:142-152`).
4. **Dispatch work**: If an `intake` queue accepts the event, an inserted event calls `intake.arrive(event)` (posting the first activity and waking the queue's worker); a previously-seen-but-unhandled event just calls `intake.wake()` (`src/linear/webhook.ts:148-150`). Otherwise `schedule` fires the `onEvent` callback without awaiting it — skipping events already in flight (tracked by `dedupeKey` in the pending-flight set) — and marks the event handled via `store.markHandled` on success, catching and journaling errors (`src/linear/webhook.ts:151`, `src/linear/webhook.ts:155-171`). So "work for the orchestrator" is the event handed to the intake queue or the `onEvent` callback as a fire-and-forget task after the database commit.

Duplicate deliveries (`committed.inserted` false and already handled) still get an `ok: true, duplicate: true` response and at most a queue wake, not a second dispatch (`src/linear/webhook.ts:148-152`). Reliability of this channel itself is monitored by `linearWebhookWarning`, which flags a `missed` webhook when the `linear:webhook-missed` cursor is newer than the last verified delivery, or a `silent` one after 60 minutes without a verified delivery while non-terminal work items exist (`src/db/linear-webhook.ts:4-29`).

answer.text:
A Linear webhook delivery becomes orchestrator work through a verify → parse → persist → dispatch pipeline in `src/linear/webhook.ts`, wired up by the server in `src/server/serve.ts`.

The flow, in order:

1. Linear POSTs to `/webhooks/linear`. The server router matches that path and calls `handleLinearWebhook(request, secrets.linearWebhookSecret, secrets.linearWebhook)`, only if webhooks are enabled and a Linear webhook secret is configured (`src/server/serve.ts:664-669`). In `src/index.ts` the production HTTP options carry `linearWebhookSecret: env.linearWebhookSecret` and `linearWebhook: linear?.webhook` where `linear.webhook` is a `LinearWebhookDeps` from the Linear runtime (`src/index.ts:965`, `src/index.ts:972`).

2. `handleLinearWebhook` verifies the delivery before any work is considered. It checks the presence and format of the `linear-signature` header (64 hex chars), the presence of the secret, and computes HMAC verification over the raw body via `checkLinearHmac` (`src/linear/webhook.ts:112-130`). The body is read through `readWebhookBody` with a 1 MiB limit and 5-second timeout, with bounds on content-length, size, and concurrent readers (`src/webhook-body/index.ts:4-46`). It also validates freshness: the timestamp is taken from the body's `webhookTimestamp` or the `linear-timestamp` header, and must pass `checkLinearTimestamp`; the docs and `TIMESTAMP_WINDOW_MS` say it must be within 60 seconds (`src/linear/webhook.ts:17`, `src/linear/webhook.ts:63-72`, `src/linear/webhook.ts:182-196`); a `linear-delivery` header is required (`src/linear/webhook.ts:139`). Failed checks return 401 (or 400 for a bad payload) and increment an in-memory failure counter; nothing is persisted (`src/linear/webhook.ts:139-144`, `src/linear/webhook.ts:177-180`).

3. The body is parsed by `parseAgentEvent` into an `AcceptedLinearEvent` containing session/issue/activity IDs, the activity body, a possible signal, metadata (actor, activity creation time), and a `dedupeKey` built from action + session/activity/delivery IDs (`src/linear/webhook.ts:198-255`, `src/linear/events.ts:9-35`). Notably, an AgentSessionEvent that looks closed (archivedAt/dismissedAt/status stopping) is treated as a `prompted` "stop" event, and a `/paws stop` body is also turned into a stop signal (`src/linear/webhook.ts:227-239`). Events other than agent sessions (e.g. Issue updates, app revocations) presumably parse to `other` actions or fail parsing, in which case the handler returns 400 `bad_payload` — only accepted events proceed.

4. Once verified, the handler records delivery health: `deps.store.setCursor(WEBHOOK_CURSOR, now)` on the `linear:webhook` sync cursor and clears the failure counter (`src/linear/webhook.ts:145-146`). This cursor is what the health check (`src/server/health.ts:118-134`) and the `linearWebhookWarning` detector (`src/db/linear-webhook.ts:15-29`) read later to see whether webhook deliveries are flowing (health fails if the cursor is older than `LINEAR_WEBHOOK_SILENCE_MS`, one hour; the UI surfaces a warning like "Linear may have disabled the Paws webhook" with a fix message (`src/db/linear-webhook.ts:4-7`, `src/db/linear-webhook.ts:31-35`)). The event is then committed via `deps.store.commit(event)`, which returns an `inserted` and `handled` flag used for dedupe (`src/linear/webhook.ts:147-151`).

5. The handler then immediately returns 200 `{ ok: true, duplicate }` to Linear. The comment says the intended design is "Verify, dedupe, commit, then 200", with follow-up work not awaited so the ack stays inside Linear's 5-second budget (`src/linear/webhook.ts:102-106`). This is exactly what the acknowledgement test asserts: every webhook body type answers 200 within 5 seconds even when the Linear client is stalled (`test/linear-webhook-ack.test.ts:63-98`).

6. Actual work is dispatched in two ways:
- If the event goes through the intake queue (`deps.intake?.accepts(event)`), a newly inserted event calls `deps.intake.arrive(event)`, which posts the first activity at once and then lets the queue's worker process it; if the event was already committed without being handled, `deps.intake.wake()` re-kicks the queue (`src/linear/webhook.ts:148-150`). Per intake-queue docs, `created` and `prompted` events go through this queue with `INTAKE_CONCURRENCY = 2`, running at once up to that limit or waiting in `inbox_event` oldest-first with escalating retry delays (`INTAKE_RETRY_MS` 30s → 10min) (`src/linear/intake-queue.ts:9-34`). Stops bypass the queue and stay immediate (`src/linear/intake-queue.ts:21-24`).
- Otherwise, `schedule(deps, event)` runs `deps.onEvent(event)` (via `flightsFor` to avoid dispatching the same `dedupeKey` twice concurrently), then calls `store.markHandled(event.dedupeKey)` on success, or logs a caught error on failure (`src/linear/webhook.ts:155-171`, `src/linear/event-dispatch.ts:1-16`).

The comment on the intake deps says "The handler only records them and wakes it" (`src/linear/webhook.ts:42-43`), and the test suite calls `openLinear(...)` with the webhook's `LinearWebhookDeps` (`test/linear-webhook-ack.test.ts:82-88`), so `openLinear` in `src/linear/runtime.ts` wires these together (`src/linear/runtime.ts:15-50`). The exact handler that consumes committed events and creates work items for the orchestrator (i.e., how `onEvent` / the intake worker turns `AcceptedLinearEvent`s into session starters or work items) is not included in the inspected evidence; the research stopped early at the deep limit, so some downstream code was not read.

Failure paths: oversized or unreadable bodies are rejected by `readWebhookBody` with 413/400/408/503 (`src/webhook-body/index.ts:1-46`); signature/timestamp/delivery problems return 401/400 with no state change except an in-memory failure count (`src/linear/webhook.ts:112-141`); a malformed payload returns 400 `bad_payload` (`src/linear/webhook.ts:141`); a missing inbox store returns 500 `not_persisted` (`src/linear/webhook.ts:142-144`); follow-up errors are logged via `journalCaught` and retried via the intake queue's delays (`src/linear/webhook.ts:165-167`, `src/linear/intake-queue.ts:13-19`).

answer.text:
A person's bypass lives in the database as a `CloseoutBypassCheck` row (who approved, why, when), is gathered into `CloseoutBypass` approvals, and then reaches the Closeout decision through `applyBypasses`, which is re-applied over the recorded evaluation when the gate re-decides the head.

The flow, as far as the evidence shows:

1. A bypass link ask carries the failed checks of a head. Those checks are stored as `closeout_bypass_check` rows via `saveCloseoutBypassChecks` and read back with `listCloseoutBypassChecks` (`src/db/closeout-bypass.ts:1-76`). The web layer surfaces them on the item page: the "Closeout needs your help" card is filled in by `withBypassChecks` (`src/web/src/live/provider.ts:1269-1326`), and `ruleDecisions` shows each offered check either as "bypassed" (when `approvedAt` is set) or "waiting" while the ask is open (`src/web/src/live/rules.ts:99-143`). A person bypasses a check on the item page, filling in the reason and their name (per the comment on `CloseoutBypassCheck` (`src/db/closeout-bypass.ts:1-76`)); `approvedBy`/`approvedByName`/`approvedAt` columns in `listCloseoutBypassChecks` (`src/db/closeout-bypass.ts:57-75`) confirm that the approval is persisted on those rows.

2. When Closeout runs again for that item, `recoveryOptions` in `src/loop/closeout-recovery.ts` collects the approvals. It walks the recorded recoveries and, only for asks whose `decision` is `"approve"`, pushes one `CloseoutBypass` per approved check (requiring `approvedBy` and `reason` to be non-null) (`src/loop/closeout-recovery.ts:37-51`). Notably, a plain reply in Linear is guidance and never bypasses a check (`src/loop/closeout-recovery.ts:23-27`), and bypasses are approved on the item page, one reason per check (`src/loop/closeout-recovery.ts:38`). The returned `{ retryBaseline, bypasses }` is how approvals leave the web/loop world — in `CloseoutGateOptions` bypasses are passed straight through as `bypasses?: GateInput["bypasses"]` (`src/closeout/gate.ts:55`).

3. The bypasses enter the gate as part of `GateInput.bypasses` (`src/closeout/run.ts:110`) / `EvaluateInput.bypasses` (`src/closeout/run.ts:69`). On a decision completion path, `decideCloseoutGate` runs no commands or review; it reconstructs the evaluation from already-recorded evidence via `decideRecorded` (`src/closeout/run.ts:469-495`). `decideRecorded` then ends by calling `finish(...)` and wrapping that with `applyBypasses(..., input.bypasses?? [])` (`src/closeout/run.ts:529-532`). The comment there says an answered pending-human check completes the evaluation the other checks finished (`src/closeout/run.ts:469-472`).

4. `applyBypasses` itself decides whether the bypass is honored. It requires the approval's `taskId`, `base`, `head`, and `policyDigest` to match the current decision, the actor and reason to be non-empty, and every requested checkId to be an item whose state is `bypassable` (that is, `"failed"`, `"exhausted"`, or `"independence"` — though an already-`"passed"` or `"skipped"` item also satisfies the approval filter) (`src/closeout/bypass.ts:21-43`). If no approval qualifies, the evaluation is returned unchanged (`src/closeout/bypass.ts:44`). Otherwise the bypassed checks are removed from the remaining set, and the outcome is recomputed: all remaining satisfied → `"accepted"`, any `"exhausted"` left → `"exhausted"`, all `"failed"` left → `"rejected"`, otherwise `"blocked"` (`src/closeout/bypass.ts:45-60`). The used approvals are attached to the evaluation as `bypasses` (`src/closeout/bypass.ts:60`) and are later summarized into the pull request body via `bypassSummary`, listing each check, its reason, and who approved it (`src/closeout/bypass.ts:63-75`).

The same `applyBypasses` is also applied right after a live evaluation completes, in `evaluateCandidate` (`applyBypasses(native, input.bypasses?? [])` (`src/closeout/run.ts:144`)), so the bypass can affect both the initial run and the later `decide` completion of a pending-human evaluation (`src/closeout/gate.ts:32-37`). After the decision, `declineCloseoutGate`... correction: `decideCloseoutGate` maps a `"rejected"` evaluation outcome to `"exhausted"` for the returned `GateOutcome` and appends to decision history when `reportDir` is set (`src/closeout/run.ts:485-494`), and `finish` independently reports `"invalid"` if an accepted decision contains unsatisfied items (`src/closeout/run.ts:1104-1111`).

Caveat on the runtime wiring: the evidence shows where bypasses leave the recovery layer (`recoveryOptions`) and where they arrive at the gate (`GateInput.bypasses`), but no inspected code shows a caller constructing `GateInput` from `recoveryOptions` output, nor the web endpoint that writes `approvedBy`/`approvedAt` onto a `closeout_bypass_check` row. Research also stopped early, so other relevant code may exist.

answer.text:
The queue start timeout is configured as `start_timeout_hours` in the `[queue]` section of `~/.paws/config.toml`. Its default is 24 hours, and the documented valid range is 1 to 720 hours (`docs/configuration.md:81`) (`src/config/file.ts:113-114`).

Configuration and default: the constant `DEFAULT_QUEUE_START_TIMEOUT_HOURS = 24` and the maximum `MAX_QUEUE_START_TIMEOUT_HOURS = 720` are defined in `src/config/queue.ts` (`src/config/queue.ts:3-4`). The type `PawsConfigFile` records that `queueStartTimeoutHours?` maps to `[queue] start_timeout_hours`, missing meaning the default of 24 (`src/config/file.ts:113-114`). Parsing of the TOML file happens in `src/config/file.ts`'s `assignConfig`, which for the `queue` section assigns `config.queueStartTimeoutHours = asInt(value, line)` for `start_timeout_hours` — so a non-integer value raises an error with the config.toml line number (`src/config/file.ts:550-553`).

Validation has two layers:

1. File-level parsing (`src/config/file.ts`): only that the value is an integer (`asInt`), failing as a numbered config.toml error (`src/config/file.ts:551`). This matches the docs' statement that an unknown key or unacceptable value stops Paws at startup with the line number and what to change (`docs/configuration.md:5`).
2. Runtime clamping (`readQueueSettings` in `src/config/queue.ts`): the value is clamped into `Math.min(Math.max(hours, 1), MAX_QUEUE_START_TIMEOUT_HOURS)` — i.e. silently clamped to the 1..720 range, missing/undefined means the 24-hour default (`src/config/queue.ts:10-13`). The companion field `maxRunningPerOwner` is treated as null (no cap) when missing or below 1, and clamped to at most `MAX_RUNNING_PER_OWNER = 1000` (`src/config/queue.ts:14-17`) (`docs/configuration.md:82`).

Another validation path applies when the value is written via the Settings form: `parseQueueSettings` in `src/config/queue.ts` rejects anything that isn't a whole number of hours from 1 to 720 with a message like `queue.startTimeoutHours must be a whole number of hours from 1 to 720`, and rejects unknown keys; a missing key keeps the stored value (`src/config/queue.ts:21-54`). The Settings HTTP handler (`src/settings/handler.ts`) merges form body values over the previous settings (or defaults 24/no cap), catches parse errors and returns them as a 400 `Invalid agent settings` response, then writes the config and audits changes like `Queue start timeout N h → M h` (`src/settings/handler.ts:104-143`). On the client side, the Settings form's `draft()` reads the `[name="queue-start-timeout"]` input, mapping an empty value to `NaN` (which is then rejected server-side), into `view.data.queue.startTimeoutHours` (`src/web/src/client/agent-settings.ts:234-240`).

Consumption: the loop orchestrator has a private `queueStartTimeoutHours()` helper that re-reads the config on every dispatch via `readQueueSettings(loadConfigFile(...))`; if the config file is unreadable, it logs via `journalCaught` and falls back to `DEFAULT_QUEUE_START_TIMEOUT_HOURS` (24) (`src/loop/orchestrator.ts:4690-4705`). Its comment says the setting is how long an item may wait for a runner slot before Paws fails it (`src/loop/orchestrator.ts:4690`); the type comment on `QueueSettings` says the same (`src/config/queue.ts:7-8`), and the docs table says the `failed` state can result from a start timeout (`docs/linear-agent-sessions.md:69`).

`writeConfigFile` also preserves the stored queue settings when re-rendering the file, calling `renderQueueSettings` with the stored `queueStartTimeoutHours` and `queueMaxRunningPerOwner` (`src/config/file.ts:279-282`).
caveats: The evidence shows parsing via asInt but no test asserting the default 24 or the 1..720 clamp; the parse-vs-clamp disagreement (parse accepts any integer, clamp only restricts at read time) is what the code does, not an assumed bug.

When a Linear intake fails, the event stays in the durable inbox store and is retried on its own backoff schedule; the whole queue only pauses for rate limits.

The intake queue (`createIntakeQueue` in `src/linear/intake-queue.ts`) runs up to `INTAKE_CONCURRENCY` (2) intakes at once, oldest first, over a SQLite-backed inbox (`src/linear/intake-queue.ts:9-10`) (`src/linear/intake-queue.ts:36-41`). Only `created` and `prompted` events that are not `stop` signals go through the queue; other events are immediate (`src/linear/intake-queue.ts:22-24`).

A failed Linear intake is not dropped — it stays in the durable SQLite inbox (`inbox_event`) and the intake queue re-delivers it on a per-event backoff schedule. Only `created`/`prompted` non-stop events go through the queue (`isQueuedIntake`, (`src/linear/intake-queue.ts:22-24`)); `createIntakeQueue`'s worker `pump()` walks `store.listQueued()` oldest first, skips events whose `nextAttemptAt` is still in the future, and caps parallel intakes at `INTAKE_CONCURRENCY = 2` (`src/linear/intake-queue.ts:73-100`). When `start()` runs `options.deliver` and it throws, the catch block decides what happens (`src/linear/intake-queue.ts:108-137`):

1. If the session entity no longer exists (`LinearEntityNotFoundError` for `AgentSession`), the event is marked handled and skipped permanently (`src/linear/intake-queue.ts:111-115`).
2. If it's a rate-limit error (`LinearRateLimitError`), the whole queue is paused via `pausedUntil`, and the event is rescheduled with `markFailed(..., counted: false)` — so a rate-limit hit doesn't consume one of the retry attempts and waits at least `INTAKE_RETRY_MS[0]` (30 s); a test confirms the wait equals `INTAKE_RETRY_MS[0]` with `attempts` staying 0 and `counted` false (`src/linear/intake-queue.ts:118-126`, `test/linear-intake-queue.test.ts:324-334`).
3. Any other error increments the attempt count (`queued.attempts + 1`) and reschedules via `intakeRetryMs(attempts)`, which walks the backoff array 30 s → 60 s → 120 s → 5 min → 10 min, staying at 10 minutes from the 5th failure onward (`src/linear/intake-queue.ts:13-19`, `src/linear/intake-queue.ts:127-136`).

Retries are independent per event: a failed event waits out its own schedule without blocking other intakes, and events in the same session/issue "lane" stay ordered (`src/linear/intake-queue.ts:36-41`, `src/linear/intake-queue.ts:79-97`). The persistence layer is `InboxStore.markFailed`, documented as recording a failed attempt where `counted: false` reschedules without spending an attempt; `QueuedLinearEvent` carries `attempts`, `nextAttemptAt`, and `lastError` (`src/linear/inbox.ts:10-32`). Once `deliver` completes, `markHandled` clears the row (`src/linear/intake-queue.ts:106-107`). The retry path is durable across restarts: a test commits an event, lets intake fail once, closes and reopens SQLite, and confirms the second delivery succeeds and creates the work item (`test/linear-intake-retry.test.ts:16-34`, `test/linear-intake-retry.test.ts:88-99`). This suggests (inference, not stated in code) that there is no terminal give-up point in the inspected evidence and a failing event repeats at 10-minute intervals.

Failures are also surfaced to the user: the status web UI renders each waiting intake entry with its attempt count, retry countdown and last error (`src/web/src/client/intake.ts:37-47`).

answer.text:
Closeout derives a finding's bug class directly from the leading text of the finding's explanation, and a finding is unclassified when that leading text is missing or too long.

The rule lives in `bugClass` in `src/closeout/rounds.ts` (`src/closeout/rounds.ts:25-29`). It runs the regex `/^\s*([^:.;\n—]+?)\s*(?::|—| - |\.|;|\n)/` over the explanation and takes the first capture group as the class — that is, everything before the first colon, em dash, " - ", period, semicolon, or newline, trimmed. So the review prompt's format "unchecked null: the handler reads …" yields the class `unchecked null` (`src/closeout/rounds.ts:21-28`). The result is lowercased, which is why "Unchecked null: e" in the tests still counts as `unchecked null` [E19:48,57].

A finding is classified `UNCLASSIFIED` (the literal string `"unclassified"` (`src/closeout/rounds.ts:16-17`)) in exactly two cases (`src/closeout/rounds.ts:27`): when the leading segment is empty (regex doesn't match or captures nothing — an empty explanation always lands here (`src/closeout/rounds.test.ts:15`)), or when the leading segment exceeds `CLASS_LIMIT = 60` characters [E1:19,27] (the test uses an 80-character lead (`src/closeout/rounds.test.ts:16`)).

Where the class is used: `recordRun` in `src/loop/review-findings.ts` calls `bugClass(finding.explanation)` on every non-blocking finding it records from an accepted head, and that value is stored in the `review_finding` table's `bug_class` column (`src/loop/review-findings.ts:109-118`, `src/db/review-findings.ts:164-186`). `upsert` refreshes `bug_class` on each later report of the same dedupe key, so the stored class tracks the most recent accepted review that mentioned the finding (`src/db/review-findings.ts:190-206`). Separately, `summarizeReviewRounds` groups review records into rounds per head (latest attempt per review per head) and, when picking the recurring bug class, skips `UNCLASSIFIED` findings entirely and picks the class reported most often, with the later round winning ties (`src/closeout/rounds.ts:59-80`). Unclassified findings still appear individually in `rounds.open` with `bugClass: "unclassified"` (`src/closeout/rounds.ts:72-79`, `src/closeout/rounds.test.ts:56-59`), and the web UI renders that class per open finding in the review-rounds card (`src/web/src/client/link-ask.ts:124-129`); the contract carries `bugClass` as a required string per open finding and `null`-able for the top-level recurring class (`src/web/src/contract.ts:1863-1872`). With no review records at all, both the rounds and the recurring class are empty/null (`src/closeout/rounds.test.ts:63-65`).

In short: classification is what the explanation starts with, up to 60 characters, before the first separator; anything else is `unclassified`, and unclassified findings are excluded from the "recurring bug class" tally but still shown on individual findings.
